html:
The Ebla tablets are an archive of some two thousand clay tablets found in 1974 and 1975 in the royal palace of Ebla, a city near Idlib in northern Syria. They date from about 2500 to 2250 BCE.

Written in cuneiform, they record the trade, taxes, treaties and rituals of a kingdom that had been forgotten. Ebla traded textiles and metals as far as Egypt and Sumer. Its language, Eblaite, is one of the oldest known Semitic languages, and the archive includes word lists in Sumerian and Eblaite, the oldest known bilingual dictionaries.

The palace was burned around 2300 BCE, which baked and saved the tablets. The find showed that northern Syria had cities and writing as old as Mesopotamia's. See also Mari and Akkad.
